summary: Specifies the NULL Authentication method and the ID_NULL identification type for IKEv2. It allows one-sided authentication or fully unauthenticated sessions when a peer cannot or will not authenticate.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7619 adds a NULL authentication method to IKEv2, the protocol that sets up encrypted VPN tunnels. A peer that uses it tells the other side plainly that it will not prove its identity. The traffic stays encrypted, but an attacker in the middle can take part in the session, so the method suits cases where encryption without identity matters more than proving who is on the other end.

questions: can ikev2 be used without authentication
subtitle: A way for an IKEv2 peer to say openly that it will not prove its identity, while keeping the session encrypted.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 could not express a peer that is unwilling or unable to authenticate itself, so a one-sided or fully anonymous key exchange could not be set up.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a NULL authentication method and an ID_NULL identification type, both with registry value 13, and states how the AUTH payload, the Peer Authorization Database and the security policy must treat them.
tldr.outcome: A peer can now run an encrypted IKEv2 session without proving who it is, which lets IKEv2 offer opportunistic encryption against pervasive monitoring, but the session is exposed to active man-in-the-middle attacks.

today: RFC 7619 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 4301 with the new Peer Authorization Database processing for NULL authentication, and it adds registry entries for the NULL authentication method and the ID_NULL identification type.

sections.title: Why Allow an Unauthenticated Peer
sections.content:
RFC 7296 gives IKEv2 a set of authentication methods, and each peer picks the method it uses to prove itself to the other side. The two peers may pick different methods, but there was no method that let one or both sides stay unauthenticated and anonymous. RFC 7619 closes that gap with a NULL authentication method and an ID_NULL identification type.

The RFC gives three situations where mutual authentication is undesirable, superfluous or impossible. A user may want an anonymous secure connection to a server, in which case the user authenticates the server but not the reverse. A sensor that wakes up and reports a measurement may need the server to authenticate the measurement but have no reason to authenticate the server. Two peers with no trust relationship may still want an encrypted channel to defend against pervasive monitoring, as described in RFC 7258, since RFC 7435 prefers unauthenticated encrypted communication over cleartext communication.

In all three cases the peer states openly that it will not certify its identity. The result is encrypted traffic without proof of who sent it.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 could not say 'I will not prove who I am'. This RFC adds that option, so a session can still be encrypted when one or both sides cannot authenticate. An attacker who can send packets can still intercept the session, so the RFC treats this as a deliberate trade-off rather than a security improvement.

sections.title: The AUTH Payload and ID_NULL
sections.content:
NULL authentication still requires a properly formed AUTH payload in the messages of the IKE_AUTH exchange, because that payload is what cryptographically links the IKE_SA_INIT exchange messages to the other messages sent over the security association.

The content of the AUTH payload is computed with the syntax used for pre-shared secret authentication. The value SK_pi for the initiator and SK_pr for the responder serve as the shared secret, so the two directions use different authentication keys. The IKEv2 Authentication Method value for NULL authentication is 13.

When a remote peer is not authenticated, any identity it sends cannot be checked. To avoid sending a made-up ID type with placeholder data, the RFC defines a new ID type, ID_NULL, whose Identification Data field must be empty. Its Identification Payload ID Type value is also 13. When anonymity matters, ID_NULL should be used; a non-null identity type with NULL authentication is acceptable for logging, troubleshooting, or when authentication happens later, out of band.

The content of the Identification payload must not be used for any trust or policy checking while NULL authentication is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The peer still sends a normal AUTH payload, computed the same way as a shared-secret authentication, so the exchange stays tied to the rest of the session. Instead of claiming an identity it cannot prove, it sends an empty one, called ID_NULL. Because that identity is unproven, the receiving side must not use it for trust or policy decisions.

sections.title: Finding Stale Security Associations
sections.content:
The identity of a peer using NULL authentication cannot be used to find existing IKE security associations created by the same peer, because the identity is not authenticated. For that reason, INITIAL_CONTACT notifications must not be used to delete any other IKE security associations on the basis of a matching peer identity, unless the implementation has separately verified that those older associations really are stale.

The standard IKE Liveness Check procedure from RFC 7296 can instead be used to detect stale IKE security associations left behind by peers that use NULL authentication. Inactive, unauthenticated associations should be checked periodically, and creating a new unauthenticated association can trigger an out-of-order check on existing ones, possibly limited to identical or close-by IP addresses or to identical identities.

Implementations should weigh the cost of sending liveness checks against the memory held by possible orphaned associations, and may treat a situation with thousands of unauthenticated associations differently from one with very few.
sections.plainLanguage: An unauthenticated peer gives no reliable name, so the usual trick of deleting older sessions that share a peer identity cannot be used. The RFC points to periodic liveness checks instead, so that abandoned sessions are found and cleaned up without trusting an unverified identity.

sections.title: The Peer Authorization Database
sections.content:
Section 4.4.3 of RFC 4301 defines the Peer Authorization Database (PAD), the ordered list of records that links the Security Policy Database to IKEv2. Each record holds peer identities, the corresponding authentication data and the data authorizing child security associations. While an IKE security association is being established, the PAD is consulted to decide how the peer should be authenticated and which child associations it may create.

RFC 7619 extends that processing in three ways. NULL authentication is added to the list of supported authentication methods, and it carries no authentication data at all. ID_NULL is added to the list of allowed ID types, and its matching rule compares only the ID type, because it holds no identity data to compare.

Each entry in the security policy database also needs a new flag saying whether unauthenticated peers may use that entry. Only rules with that flag turned on can be used for unauthenticated connections, and implementations must not mix authenticated and unauthenticated rules. Appendix A of the RFC lists the exact edits to make in Section 4.4.3 of RFC 4301.
sections.plainLanguage: The PAD is the list that says how each peer should be authenticated and what it is allowed to set up. This RFC adds NULL authentication to that list as a method with no key material, and adds an entry for the empty identity that matches on type alone. Each policy entry also needs a switch that says whether unauthenticated peers may use it.

sections.title: Traffic Selectors and Unauthenticated Peers
sections.content:
Traffic Selectors and narrowing let two IKE peers agree on a traffic range for an IPsec security association. An unauthenticated peer must not be able to use that mechanism to steal traffic that another peer intended for a different host. The problem is sharpest with anonymous peers behind NAT, because such a peer builds an IPsec security association using its pre-NAT IP address, which differs from the source IP of its IKE packets.

The RFC's example: if the remote host uses 192.0.2.1 as its DNS server, a rogue IKE peer could set its Traffic Selector to 192.0.2.1 in an attempt to receive the remote host's DNS traffic. Implementations should restrict and isolate all anonymous IKE peers from each other and from themselves, allowing such a peer access only to itself and possibly to its intended network ranges.

One way to achieve this is to always assign internal IP addresses to unauthenticated IKE clients, as described in Section 2.19 of RFC 7296. Implementations may also use internal NAT and connection tracking. Implementations may force unauthenticated peers onto single host-to-host IPsec security associations. Because that is not always possible with IPv6, implementations must be able to assign a full /64 address block to the peer, as described in RFC 5739, even when the peer is not authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer that cannot be identified might try to claim traffic that belongs to someone else. The RFC says to isolate such peers from each other, give them internal addresses instead of real ones, and restrict what they may encrypt. With IPv6 the RFC goes further: the peer must be given a whole /64 address block of its own.

sections.title: Assumptions That No Longer Hold
sections.content:
If authenticated IKE sessions are possible for a given Traffic Selector range between two peers, then unauthenticated IKE should not be allowed for that range, and policy rules should ensure the highest available level of security is used between them. If both peers use NULL authentication, the whole key exchange becomes unauthenticated and the session is vulnerable to active man-in-the-middle attacks. Using an ID type other than ID_NULL with NULL authentication may compromise the client's anonymity in such an attack.

Because the session no longer proves who it is talking to, any logging of unproven ID payloads should be clearly marked as untrusted and possibly accompanied by the remote IP address of the session, with rate limiting on the logging.

The denial-of-service countermeasures described in RFC 7296 and in the work on protecting IKE from distributed denial of service do not account for peers that are allowed to stay unauthenticated, because such a peer is a fully legitimate IKE peer that differs only in having used NULL authentication. Implementations must not assume peers are friendly, trusted or identifiable, and must handle abusive unauthenticated peers, for example one sending a flood of liveness probes or delete requests.

Two further rules follow. An unauthenticated peer must not reach resources meant only for authenticated peers, and must not be able to replace the child security associations of an authenticated peer. And because ESP (protocol 50) or ESP-in-UDP (UDP port 4500) packets do not match packet filters written for unencrypted traffic, peers that support unauthenticated IKE must pass all decrypted traffic through the same packet filters and security mechanisms as incoming plaintext traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Supporting an unauthenticated peer means dropping assumptions that a peer is known and well behaved. The RFC spells out the consequences: the session can be attacked from the middle, denial-of-service defences must assume the attacker is a legitimate client, unauthenticated peers must not reach authenticated-only resources, and decrypted traffic must still pass the same firewall checks as plain traffic.

sections.title: New Registry Entries
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to add one entry to each of two registries. In the IKEv2 Authentication Method registry, value 13 is assigned to NULL authentication. In the IKEv2 Identification Payload ID Types registry, value 13 is assigned to ID_NULL. Both registries therefore use the same number for the two new values.

The RFC also updates RFC 4301, adding the processing rules for NULL authentication to the PAD section of that document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new values are registered, both numbered 13: the NULL authentication method and the ID_NULL identity type. The document also amends the earlier IPsec security architecture document to describe how the peer authorization list handles them.
